opening.headline: Learn how to determine where in-house AI use cases are permitted and prohibited based on the common framework of the three providers' policies.
body: There are many candidates for in-house AI applications, such as customer service chatbots, initial screening of resumes, drafting sales emails, and assisting with insurance claims reviews. However, each provider's policy document is long and worded differently. Even in the same case, judgments seem to differ depending on which clause of the document is read.

In this lesson, we'll place the table of contents of Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google's usage policies side-by-side and map out common prohibited categories and additional requirements attached to high-risk uses. Next, we check the responsibilities of those who create and use the product, and guidelines related to minors, and classify customer service chatbots and employment screening cases using the same criteria.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Describe common prohibited categories in the three providers' usage policies and additional requirements for high-risk usage
You can distinguish criteria for classifying internal use cases as permitted, conditional, or prohibited.

screens.title: How far is permitted and where is prohibited?
screens.lead:
There are four candidates for AI applications that we are considering in-house. Select a card one by one to see why each candidate hesitates when reading their policies.

Policy base date: 2026-10-23. Distinguish between the version currently in effect and the version scheduled to be implemented. Anthropic has released the 2026-11-12 enforcement version, so you should check again for changes in the enforcement date and high-risk areas and disclosure obligations before actual operation.

items.answer: This is a consumer chatbot that provides delivery and refund information. Although it may seem like general information, the fact that it speaks directly to consumers and that it can be used by minors may be treated as separate conditions in the policy.

It is an auxiliary tool for filtering out applicants. It may seem like ordinary automation that improves work efficiency, but it is an area that policy pays special attention to because it is a decision that affects people's employment opportunities.

The model drafts emails for sales representatives. It is a general task where people read and edit before sending, so the burden is relatively low, but you must be careful not to include phrases that can be read as impersonation or deception.

It is a tool to help the person in charge of determining whether insurance claims will be paid. This is an area where policy places additional demands because the results directly affect the economic interests of individuals.

The documents from the three providers are long and worded differently, so the same case appears to be judged differently in each document. But if we have a common framework for policies, wouldn't we be able to classify cases using the same criteria in any document? This lesson begins with finding the skeleton.

screens.outro: First, let me recall an experience where I had similar concerns.

screens.title: Map of norms surrounding AI
screens.lead: Select the numbered markers in the picture one by one to see what each floor decides and who decides. The final marker is a framework that organizes the activities that manage these layers within the organization. Also check out which floors this class reads in detail.

visual.alt: A five-layer map with laws and regulations, provider usage policies, model principles of conduct, safety framework, and internal organizational policies stacked from top to bottom, with four activity brackets on the right.

markers.label: Laws and regulations
markers.title: 1st floor. laws and regulations
markers.body: It is determined by national and local laws. Representative examples include personal information protection laws and sector-specific regulations. It is not something an organization can choose; it applies regardless of which product is used, and if violated, legal liability is imposed. Even if the provider's policy allows it, it cannot be used if the law prohibits it, and conversely, even if the law allows it, the lower floors may be blocked more narrowly.

markers.label: Provider usage policy
markers.title: 2nd floor. Provider usage policy
markers.body: These are the usage policies and terms set by the provider as conditions for using the service. It contains additional requirements attached to prohibited categories and high-risk uses. A characteristic of this layer is that the provider can prohibit actions that are permitted by law. This is the layer that this class reads in the most detail.

markers.label: model behavior principles
markers.title: 3rd floor. model behavior principles
markers.body: Like the Model Specification or Constitution, it is a public document that explains how the model makes decisions and what requests it rejects. While usage policies are the rules we require from users, this layer is the standards the model wants itself to follow. In the same service, it serves as the basis for explaining why the model follows certain requests and rejects others.

markers.label: safety framework
markers.title: 4th floor. Frontier Safety Framework
markers.body: It is a framework disclosed by the provider on how to evaluate the serious risks that a very capable model can create and under what conditions its distribution is limited. We address risks in the development and deployment phases of the model rather than in individual use cases. Organizations read this framework to understand under what protections the model they wish to adopt is provided.

markers.label: Organizational internal policies and controls
markers.title: 5th floor. Organizational internal policies and controls
markers.body: This is a floor directly determined by our organization. This includes acceptable and prohibited practices, approval procedures, data handling standards, and audit evidence. Since the above four layers are norms that we have not set, the role of this layer is to translate them into specific examples of our services.

markers.label: NIST AI RMF
markers.title: Organizational Management Activities: The Four Functions of the NIST AI RMF
markers.body: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (NIST AI 100-1, 2023) divides the activities through which organizations address AI risk into four categories: **Govern** is the activity of establishing responsibility and policy system, **Map** is the activity of understanding the context of use and identifying risks, **Measure** is the activity of analyzing, evaluating and tracking risks, and **Manage** is the activity of setting priorities and responding. It is a framework that is used voluntarily rather than by law, and there is also a separate profile (NIST AI 600-1) tailored to generative AI. In the same context, ISO/IEC 42001 is an international standard that sets requirements for organizations developing, providing, and using AI to establish and maintain a responsible AI management system.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed the location of this class on the map, let's first recall an experience where we had similar concerns.

screens.title: Think of a similar situation
screens.lead: If you think about the question on your own first and then select it, the instructor will organize it for you. You will not enter or submit an answer. Read and compare it with your own experience.

items.prompt: When planning a new AI feature, have you ever hesitated and wondered, ‘Can I do this?’
items.answer: If you check the policy after creating a function, the design has already solidified and is difficult to change. The best time to read the policy is at the beginning of planning. If you know the classification criteria you learn in this class, instead of hesitating, the question changes to what conditions you need to meet.

items.prompt: Have you ever read a policy document and gotten confused about which section your case is?
items.answer: Policy documents are a mix of listing prohibited activities, dividing them by user type, and dividing them into risk areas. If the structure is different, it is difficult to find the same case. That's why it's helpful to put documents side by side and find a common framework.

items.prompt: Are there any scenes where it was unclear who was responsible, the person who created the service or the person who used it?
items.answer: Both organizations that create products based on the provider's model and end users who use those products are subject to the policy. If responsibility is placed on only one side, a loophole is created. This is covered in more detail in the Accountability screen.

screens.outro: Now, let’s compare the structures by placing the policy contents of the three providers side by side.

screens.title: Putting the three companies’ policies side by side
screens.lead: Select a tab to see how the policies of the three providers are structured. The last tab organizes common skeletons.

tabs.label: Anthropic
tabs.body:
Anthropic's usage policy is **three-pronged** depending on the user and purpose.
- **Universal Usage Criteria**: Applies to all users and use cases.
- **High-Risk Use Requirements**: Applies to high-risk use cases that directly impact consumers.
- **Additional Use Case Guidance**: Applies to consumer chatbots, minor-facing products, agent usage, MCP servers, etc.

The scope of application is also wide. This includes individual users of the app, developers and enterprises using the API, customers using the cloud or reseller, and even end users of integrated products.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body:
OpenAI's usage policy is centered around the principle of protecting people. Representative items include protecting people, protecting minors, and ensuring human autonomy.

The autonomy section prohibits manipulation and deception and prohibits automatically making high-stakes decisions in sensitive areas without human review. The view is that people should be involved in decisions that affect their interests.

tabs.label: Google
tabs.body:
Our prohibited use policy consists of **four categories**:
1. Dangerous or illegal activities
2. Activities that violate service security
3. Sexual, violent and hateful activities
4. False or deceptive acts

The peculiarity is that it leaves exceptions open. Exceptions may be made for educational, documentary, scientific, or artistic considerations, or when the public interest outweighs the harm.

tabs.label: common skeleton
tabs.body:
Although the structures of the three documents are different, the major framework of the ban overlaps.
- Prohibition of use that causes **illegal and harmful**
- **Security infringement** prohibited
- **Hate and harassment** prohibited
- **Deception and impersonation** prohibited

Additionally, all three require human oversight in areas that significantly impact individuals. If you look at examples based on this skeleton rather than the document structure, you can classify the document in the same way no matter which document you read. Even if the wording varies from document to document, it is important to get into the habit of asking which category the case falls into.

screens.outro: Let's take a look at what each category of common framework specifically includes.

screens.title: Contents of common prohibited categories
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom to see what actions are included in each common prohibited category.

data.caption: Prohibited categories common to the three provider policies
rows: Content related to child sexual exploitation, promotion of violent extremism and terrorism, promotion of self-harm, non-consensual intimate images
Is there any possibility that the output of my case could create or spread this content?
Infringement of the rights of others
Use of personal information and biometric information without consent, tracking and surveillance without consent
Is there consent from the parties regarding the personal information covered by the case?
Spam, phishing, malware, infrastructure disruption, or model manipulation to bypass safety filters.
Can the case be used to circumvent the protections of a system or service?
Fraud, impersonation, man-made misrepresentation, or misinformation about political processes such as elections.
Does the source and identity of the output be truthfully indicated?
OpenAI explicitly prohibits personal evaluations (social scoring) based on social behavior or biometric information, and emotional inferences in workplaces and educational settings.
Does the case include the function of inferring and evaluating a person's tendencies or emotions?
data.notes: Content related to child sexual exploitation is prohibited in all three locations. Since the personal evaluation category is an item specified in the OpenAI policy, you must check the individual document to see if the same expression is present in other provider policies. The difference from high-risk use, which we will see next, is that if it falls into the prohibited category, it is not permitted even if conditions are met. The last column of the table can be used verbatim as a check question when reviewing cases in-house. A case can span multiple categories, so you need to check them all line by line. For example, if your sales email drafting tool collects recipients' personal information, you should also check for infringement categories.

screens.outro: Let's look at high-risk use, which is an area that, unlike prohibition, can be used if conditions are met.

screens.title: High-Risk Use and Additional Requirements
screens.lead: The following flashcards illustrate the demands attached to high-risk use. When you select a card, it flips over and you can move to the next card with the right arrow.

cards.back: Anthropic identifies high-risk uses as legal, medical, insurance, financial, employment and housing, academic assessment and admissions, and professional media content. This is because these areas are considered important for public welfare and social equity and therefore pose a high risk to individuals and consumers. High risk is an area that is not prohibited but permitted with additional measures.

Any advice, recommendation or subjective judgment affecting an individual or consumer should be reviewed by a qualified professional in the relevant field before any content or decision is conveyed or confirmed. The service operator is responsible for the accuracy and appropriateness of the content. This means that the draft created by the model should not be formally handed over to an expert, but should be checked by someone who can actually judge it.

cards.front: Additional Demand 2. Disclosure of AI Use
cards.back: If the model's output is visible directly to an individual or consumer, it must be communicated that the advice or decision was made with the help of AI. This instruction should be given at least at the beginning of each session. Consumers should be informed at the beginning of the conversation, rather than once in the middle of a consultation.

Consumer-facing chatbots or externally-facing AI agents, regardless of whether they are high-risk, must inform users that they are talking to an AI rather than a human. This disclosure is also made at least at the beginning of each chat session. Even if you use a name or tone that looks like a human counselor, you should not hide the fact that you are an AI.

Google prohibits automated decisions that significantly disadvantage individuals' rights without human oversight in high-risk areas such as employment, healthcare, finance, legal, housing, insurance, and social services. OpenAI also prohibits automating high-risk decisions in sensitive areas without human review. Although the expressions are different, the three points to the same point.

screens.outro: Next, we'll look at who the policy targets and what changes when minors are involved.

screens.title: Operator and End User Responsibilities, Minor Instructions
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to compare what your policy covers and any additional requirements when minors are involved.

states.label: operator and end user
states.body:
The policy applies to both the operator who creates and provides the product and the end user of the product. The organization that created the chatbot using the provider's model is responsible for designing the chatbot to ensure that it does not violate policies, and people who use the chatbot must not use it for purposes that violate policies.

Google advises that developers are responsible for safely applying their models. This means that even if the provider has installed a safety device in the model, the manufacturer of the product is responsible for the safety of the product made on it. Don't skip product-level inspection, expecting the model to take care of it for you.

So when we review in-house use cases, we divide into what we as operators will do and what the end users will do. For example, operators should have measures in place at the design stage to detect and limit end users from using the chatbot for purposes that violate policy.

states.label: Guidelines for Minors
states.body:
Services that work directly with minors require additional safeguards. Age verification, content filtering, monitoring and reporting systems, and user guidance materials should be in place. They must also comply with relevant regulations (e.g. COPPA in the US) and inform users that they are talking to AI.

OpenAI requires that zero data retention be applied to APIs before processing personal information of children under the age of 13. Google's API Additional Terms state that you must be 18 years of age or older to use the API.

Therefore, if your target audience is likely to include minors, this need should be identified early in the service design. Adding age verification and reporting systems after completion is much more expensive.

screens.outro: Now let's group the elements so far into case classification criteria.

screens.title: Explanation: Criteria for dividing use cases into permitted, conditional, and prohibited
screens.lead: The instructor explains how to classify a case using four questions: Select the arrows to follow the questions in order.

steps.title: Question 1. Is this a category that is forbidden to everyone?
steps.body: First, we look to see if it falls into a category that is unacceptable to any user, such as illegal, harmful, deceptive, or a security breach. If applicable, it is prohibited without any other conditions. The reason I put this question first is because the questions that follow are only meaningful in cases where they can be accepted if the conditions are met. For example, email tools intended for impersonation are not permitted, even with human review.

steps.title: Question 2. Does it affect individuals in high-risk areas?
steps.body: We look at areas that affect people's important interests, such as law, medicine, finance, employment, insurance, and housing. If applicable, you will become a conditional candidate subject to additional requirements such as expert review and disclosure of AI use. The list of areas varies slightly from provider to provider, so we compare directly in the documentation which areas our cases fall into.

steps.title: Question 3. Does it come into contact with consumers or minors?
steps.body: Check whether the service communicates directly with consumers and whether minors can use it. Where applicable, you must verify claims such as AI disclosure, age verification, and filtering. This question applies separately even if it is not a high-risk area. Questions 2 and 3 are independent and may both apply.

steps.title: Question 4: Is it possible to have measures in place?
steps.body: See if we can actually have human review and disclosure of AI usage. If you can have it, you should allow it conditionally, and if you can't have it, you should stop using it. The riskiest thing is to proceed with conditional use without a plan to take action.

steps.title: Read classification results
steps.body: If question 1 applies, it is prohibited. If questions 2 or 3 are met and the measures in question 4 are in place, then conditional acceptance is possible. If none of the questions apply, it is considered acceptable. This order serves as an internal checklist to ensure that different documents are read to the same standard by each provider. Placing your case on this checklist will help you know ahead of time what actions and costs will be required during the planning stage.

screens.outro: Now that we have established the standard, let's apply it to the first case, a customer service chatbot.

screens.title: Commentary: Policy interpretation of customer service chatbots
screens.lead: The instructor classifies consumer chatbots that guide delivery and refunds step by step according to the preceding criteria. Skip the steps with the arrows.

steps.title: scenario
steps.body: This is a service where a chatbot answers when consumers ask about delivery status and refund policies. This does not apply to question 1 as it is far from illegal or deceptive. Even if customer information is handled, the purpose is not tracking or monitoring without consent, so it is far from the category of rights infringement. The first step is to compare the prohibited categories one by one.

steps.title: Face-to-face verification with consumers
steps.body: Since this is a chatbot that deals directly with consumers, users must be informed at the beginning of the session that it is AI. This demand applies to all consumer chatbots, regardless of whether they are high-risk or not.

steps.title: Check range
steps.body: The refund policy is provided as a general guide only. However, if the conversation moves into legal judgment or insurance review, it enters high-risk territory, so when the chatbot receives such questions, its scope is limited to human consultation. Politely decline out-of-scope questions and plan a response in advance that guides the responsible department.

steps.title: Minor Verification
steps.body: If there is a possibility that a minor may use it, we review age verification and filtering. Lifestyle services such as delivery and refunds are also areas frequently used by teenagers. If the target audience according to the Terms of Service is an adult, that fact and the method of confirmation are made clear. We assume that minors can use services that do not go through a verification process and filter them out. This is because even if the target audience for consumer services is narrowly defined, the actual users can be broader.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: It is allowed, but it is a conditional permit with restrictions on the disclosure and scope of AI use. At first it may seem like a simple permit, but conditions such as consumer contact points and scope limitations must be checked. Documenting the conditions like this will help you know which items to check again later when you expand your scope of services.

screens.outro: Next, let's look at a case where judgment is more weighty: hiring screening.

screens.title: Commentary: Policy Interpretation of Employment Screening
screens.lead: An assistant tool for reading resumes and filtering out applicants, sorted by the same criteria. Use the arrows to move through the steps and compare what is different from the chatbot example.

steps.title: scenario
steps.body: It is an auxiliary tool that reads resumes and filters out applicants who do not fit the job. The goal is to speed up processing, so it looks like simple task automation. However, the results lead to job opportunities for individual applicants.

steps.title: Identify high risk areas
steps.body: Anthropic positions hiring as a high-risk use, citing resume screening and recruiting tools as examples. This clearly applies to question 2, so it's not for general use. In the chatbot example, question 2 could have varied depending on the flow of the conversation, but this is high-risk territory from the start.

steps.title: Expressions from other providers
steps.body: Google prohibits automated decisions without human oversight that significantly disadvantage individual rights in high-risk areas, including employment. OpenAI also prohibits automating high-risk decisions in sensitive areas without human review. The three conclusions are the same. This also means that your needs do not disappear even if you change providers.

steps.title: Required Action
steps.body: Results must be reviewed by a responsible expert before finalizing them, and applicants must be informed that AI has helped them. The demands are heavier than in the chatbot case. This is because the results of the judgment directly affect an individual’s employment opportunities. If the reviewer simply follows the tool's decisions, it is difficult to call it a human review.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: The way the tool automatically determines elimination is close to prohibitive. Conditionally permitted only for auxiliary uses that assist the human judgment process. Even for the same tool, the classification varies depending on who has decision-making authority. The design should reflect the structure suggested by the tool and determined by people.

screens.outro: Finally, we organize the entire class. Remember that in both cases, it wasn't the technology that made the difference, but the impact and actionability of the decision.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: We organize the common structure and case classification criteria of the three provider policies into one.

paragraphs: Although the three providers' policies are structured differently, they have common prohibition categories of illegality and harm, security violations, hate and harassment, and deception. If you fall into this category, you will not be accepted even if conditions are met.

High-risk uses are not prohibited, but rather conditional areas. It can be used if it has expert review and disclosure of AI use, and automatic decisions without human supervision are prohibited in all three places. The policy applies to both the operator who created the product and the end user, and services that serve minors require additional safeguards such as age verification and filtering. Rather than re-reading the entire document every time the policy changes, it is more efficient to check for changes to this framework.

Cases are classified in the following order: confirmation of prohibited category, presence of high-risk areas, contact points between consumers and minors, and possibility of action. The answer to the first question, whether cases can be classified by the same criteria if a common framework of policy is established, is that it is possible. Even if the document is long and the expressions are different, the skeletons overlap.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Think about which AI use cases in your work could be classified as conditional, and whether those conditions are currently in place. If you don't have it, think about what you need to prepare first.

The expert in charge reviews it before confirmation and informs the applicant of AI assistance.
Resume screening is a prohibited category and cannot be used in any form.
Skip human review only when there are a large number of applicants

Does it affect individuals in high-risk areas such as legal, medical, financial, and employment?
Can it be communicated directly with consumers or used by minors?

glossary.def: This is a document that summarizes actions that the provider prohibits or imposes conditions on when using the product.
Uses that have a significant impact on individuals and require additional action, such as legal, medical, financial, or employment.
An organization that integrates the provider's model into its own product and provides it to end users.
This is where a decision is reviewed by a qualified person before it is finalized.
It lets consumers know that they are interacting with AI or that AI was used to generate an outcome.
It is a voluntary framework that helps organizations manage AI risks by dividing them into four functions: Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.

misconceptions.fact: High-risk use is an area where it is acceptable with additional measures in place, such as human review and disclosure of AI use. It must be distinguished from the prohibited category.

misconceptions.myth: Only developers need to adhere to the policy.
misconceptions.fact: The policy applies to both operators who create products and end users who use the products.

misconceptions.myth: The policies of the three companies are completely different.
misconceptions.fact: The large framework of the prohibited categories overlaps and differs only in detailed expression and document structure. Based on their common skeleton, they can be classified in the same way.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Common prohibited categories are illegal and harmful, security breach, hateful and harassing, and deceptive.
High-risk uses come with additional requirements, such as human review and disclosure of AI use.
The responsibilities of the operator and end users and the protection of minors are checked separately.
Cases are classified in the following order: prohibited, high risk, contact, and actionable.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Which AI use cases in my business can be classified as conditional, and what action do I need to take?
